subtitle: Recognize harassment and disrespectful conduct, consider bystander responses, and develop team practices that support speaking up. Learn how to raise concerns with the person or area responsible.
audience: For all DHS and DSD employees, including supervisors, who want shared language and practical options for a respectful workplace. It does not replace HR, EOAD or legal advice.

lessons.title: What harassment and a respectful workplace mean
objectives: Distinguish the legal definition of harassment from the broader conduct standard in state respectful workplace policy.
Identify the protected classes named in federal law and in the Minnesota Human Rights Act.
Explain why an employee does not have to decide which policy applies before raising a concern.
Recognize examples of disrespectful conduct named in state policy, including deliberate misgendering and deliberate mispronunciation of names.
lessons.teaching:
Workplace concerns can involve federal law, Minnesota law and agency policy, each with a different scope. The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission describes harassment as unwelcome conduct based on a protected characteristic such as race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age forty and older, disability or genetic information. Under federal law it becomes illegal when putting up with it becomes a condition of keeping the job, or when it is severe or pervasive enough that a reasonable person would find the workplace intimidating, hostile or abusive. The EEOC is clear that petty slights and isolated incidents, unless extremely serious, usually do not reach that legal line.

Minnesota law includes protections that extend beyond federal employment discrimination law, including additional protected classes. The Minnesota Department of Human Rights lists race, religion, disability, national origin, sex, marital status, familial status, age, sexual orientation and gender identity among the protected classes, and the Act also prohibits reprisal against people who assert their rights. Age protection under state law starts at the age of majority rather than at forty.

State and agency policies also establish expectations for daily conduct. Minnesota Management and Budget sets statewide human resources policies for executive branch agencies. Its Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited policy covers unwelcome conduct tied to protected class, including offensive jokes, slurs, and deliberate misgendering or mispronunciation of a name. Its Respectful Workplace policy covers disrespectful conduct that is not tied to protected class: shouting, threats, demeaning or humiliating treatment, bullying, and sabotaging someone's work. DHS has its own policies that follow the same pattern. Conduct can violate these policies without meeting the legal standard for unlawful harassment. Staff can raise a concern without first proving a legal violation.

You do not have to decide whether something is illegal harassment, a policy violation or just a bad day before you raise it. Sorting that out is the job of Human Resources and the DHS Equal Opportunity and Access Division. Your job is to notice, to respond in a way that is safe, and to route the concern to people who can act. These explanations support a factual referral rather than an independent investigation or a legal determination by the person raising the concern.
lessons.keyPoint: Conduct may violate workplace policy without meeting the legal standard for unlawful harassment. Raise the facts through the designated route; HR and EOAD assess which process applies.
lessons.example: Practice case: In a DSD policy team meeting, a staff member repeatedly uses an unwanted nickname for a coworker who has asked him to stop. He jokes that her full name is too hard, then mocks her accent in a message thread. Another team member witnesses both exchanges but hesitates to raise a concern because she is unsure which policy applies.
lessons.question: How should the team member approach the conduct she observed?
choices: Wait until she is certain the conduct meets the legal definition of harassment before saying anything.
Recognize that the conduct may fall under state policy whether or not it is illegal, and that she can raise it without deciding which category it fits.
Decide it is only rudeness, since one nickname and one joke are isolated incidents.
feedback: You can raise the observed conduct without first proving unlawful harassment. Follow the designated reporting route so the responsible office can assess it.

This response describes the conduct without deciding the legal outcome. State policies address repeated or deliberate misuse of a name, and comments connected to protected class may also fall under the harassment policy. The team member can raise what she observed through the designated route.

Repeated conduct after a request to stop is not an isolated incident, and conduct linked to national origin may fall under the harassment policy. The witness should not dismiss the concern on the coworker’s behalf.
lessons.reflection: Think about a time you hesitated to name something at work because you were not sure it was serious enough. What would have helped you feel able to raise it without first having to judge it?
lessons.action: Find the current DHS respectful workplace and harassment and discrimination policies on the DHS intranet or through your HR contact. Note in your own words one example of conduct each policy names, and where each policy says to report.

check.question: Why do state respectful workplace and harassment policies reach conduct that may not be illegal?
check.correct: So the employer can address and correct harmful conduct early, before it becomes severe or pervasive.
wrong: Because state policy replaces federal law for state employees.
Because every rude comment is illegal under the Minnesota Human Rights Act.
check.feedback: Policy is intentionally set above the legal floor. It lets supervisors, HR and EOAD address conduct early. It does not replace federal law, and not every rude act is illegal. The value of the policy is that you can raise a concern without proving a legal case.

lessons.title: Bystander action: the five Ds at work
objectives: Describe the five bystander strategies: distract, delegate, document, delay and direct.
Choose a bystander response that fits the safety, setting and wishes of the person targeted.
Distinguish consent-based bystander guidance from workplace reporting and records responsibilities.
Identify how a supervisor's duty to report changes what bystander action looks like for them.
lessons.teaching:
Bystander action offers ways to support someone while responding to conduct you have observed. Right To Be teaches five options: distract, delegate, document, delay and direct. Its guidance emphasizes safety and the wishes of the person targeted. The workplace examples below adapt those options to DHS work, where reporting duties and rules for handling records also apply.

Distract means interrupting the exchange without confronting the person responsible for the conduct. In a meeting, you might ask a work question or suggest a short break. Delegate means seeking help from someone positioned to act, such as the meeting chair or a supervisor. Describe what you observed and what help you need without deciding another person's motive or asking the helper to conduct an informal investigation.

Document means recording relevant facts, such as the date, words used and people present, while considering safety and whether support is already available. Right To Be advises asking the targeted person how they want documentation used and obtaining permission before sharing it. That guidance does not override DHS reporting, retention or data-handling responsibilities. Keep workplace notes factual and protected, explain the sharing your role requires, and use the authorized process. Do not promise that a person's preference can prevent every required disclosure or determine what happens to an agency record.

Delay means offering support after the incident, including asking what the person needs and whether they want help finding a reporting route. A quiet response or a switched-off camera does not establish how someone feels, so ask without assigning an experience to them. Direct means briefly naming the conduct when it is safe and likely to help. Consider the risk of escalation and whether another option would provide more useful support.

Bystander support and reporting have different purposes, and one does not replace the other. DHS policy expects employees to report complaints promptly to a supervisor or Equal Opportunity and Access. Supervisors have additional immediate reporting and referral responsibilities under statewide and agency procedures. Explain those responsibilities rather than promising secrecy, even when someone prefers a private resolution. A contract manager may need to address contractor conduct, but contacting that manager does not replace the applicable complaint route.

You can listen, describe what you observed and ask about immediate support without investigating the allegation yourself. Do not interview colleagues or decide whether the account is credible before making a required referral. Someone who was affected can express preferences about support and participation, while the agency remains responsible for decisions within its authority. Follow up on what you agreed to do without promising a finding or a particular outcome.
lessons.keyPoint: Choose a response that considers safety, the setting and the person’s support preferences. Explain and follow applicable reporting duties; bystander support does not replace the authorized complaint process.
lessons.example: Practice case: During a video call with county partners, a DHS contractor makes a joke about a program participant’s religion. The DSD staff member organizing the call notices a colleague turn off her camera but does not know why. The organizer is not a supervisor, and several partners are senior to her. Afterward, she considers how to offer support and address the conduct she heard.
lessons.question: What is the most helpful response after the call?
choices: Check in privately with the colleague, ask what support she wants, explain the applicable reporting responsibilities, and raise the observed conduct through the designated agency route.
Email the contractor and all county partners with an account of the colleague’s reaction so everyone knows the comment was unacceptable.
Keep the incident entirely private unless the colleague asks for a report, because the organizer is not a supervisor.
feedback: This response offers support without deciding what the colleague experienced or promising secrecy. The organizer follows the applicable complaint route and can consult the contract manager about contractor responsibilities without substituting that contact for reporting.

A broad email may disclose more than the authorized response requires and assign meaning to the colleague’s behavior. Raise the observed conduct through the designated route and ask about support privately.
DHS reporting expectations are not limited to supervisors. The organizer should explain the applicable responsibilities and follow them while respecting the colleague’s choices about support.
lessons.reflection: Which of the five Ds feels most natural to you, and which feels hardest? What would make the hardest one easier to use in your actual meetings?
lessons.action: Write down two short phrases you could use in a meeting to distract or direct, and one sentence you could use to check in with a coworker afterward. Keep them somewhere you will see them before your next large meeting.

check.question: According to Right To Be, what should a bystander do with a recording or note of a harassment incident?
check.correct: Ask the person who was targeted what they want done with it, and not share it without their permission.
wrong: Post it so others can see the behavior was witnessed.
Keep it private and never mention it to anyone, including the person targeted.
check.feedback: Right To Be’s guidance centers the targeted person’s wishes when using documentation. In DHS work, explain and follow applicable reporting and records responsibilities as well. A supportive conversation must not promise confidentiality or control over agency action that your role cannot provide.

lessons.title: Psychological safety as team practices
objectives: Explain Amy Edmondson's definition of team psychological safety.
Distinguish psychological safety from comfort, niceness or lowered standards.
Identify at least four observable practices that build or erode psychological safety on a team.
Plan how a leader takes responsibility for repair after a comment or decision lands badly.
lessons.teaching:
Amy Edmondson, a researcher at Harvard Business School, defined team psychological safety as a shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking. Interpersonal risks are ordinary work acts that could make someone look ignorant, incompetent or disruptive: asking a question, admitting a mistake, raising a concern or disagreeing with a more senior person. In her study of work teams in a manufacturing company, psychological safety was associated with more learning behavior, and learning behavior was associated with better team performance. The study supports an association; it does not establish that a particular team practice will cause better performance in every setting.

Psychological safety is not the same as being nice, avoiding conflict or lowering expectations. A team can hold high standards and still make it safe to say that something is not working. Questions and accurate information help a team examine whether its work meets the standards it has set. It is also a team-level condition. It describes how a group works, not a personality trait that some staff have and others lack.

The following are program practice suggestions for making concerns discussable, not a guarantee of psychological safety. Before deciding, ask what evidence or concerns challenge your proposal, and acknowledge useful contributions in a way the person is comfortable with. Respond to uncertainty with useful information, while recognizing that lack of harmful intent does not rule out a policy violation. Route possible violations through the applicable process without first deciding what the person intended. Put repair on the person with more power: when a comment or decision lands badly, the leader names it and takes responsibility, and the person harmed is not asked to explain, educate or forgive on a schedule. Show that input changed something: regularly say what changed because someone spoke up, and if nothing did, say why. Examine workload and timing: repeated urgency may limit opportunities to think or raise concerns, so make room for questions before decisions.

These practices do not replace reporting duties or formal channels, whose confidentiality limits still apply. A team with good habits still routes complaints of harassment and discrimination to HR and EOAD. A supportive response may encourage people to raise concerns, but silence does not establish that a team is safe. It does not make the supervisor an investigator.
lessons.keyPoint: Psychological safety is a shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk taking. Team practices, including leaders’ responses to disagreement, mistakes and harm, can support speaking up.
lessons.example: Practice case: A supervisor leads a DSD waiver policy team. In a planning meeting, she dismisses a newer analyst’s concern that a notice will confuse families, saying there is no time to revisit it. Two weeks later, a county partner raises the same problem. The supervisor notices that the analyst has stopped contributing in meetings, but she has not asked why. She wants to address her decision without putting him on the spot.
lessons.question: What should the supervisor do next?
choices: Tell the analyst privately that he should speak up more, since his concerns are clearly valuable.
Wait for the analyst to raise the issue himself so he can decide whether it needs attention.
Check how the analyst would like his contribution acknowledged, then tell the team she dismissed an important concern, explain the notice change and state how she will handle concerns in future.
feedback: Encouragement alone places the responsibility on the analyst without addressing the supervisor’s earlier decision. She can ask about his experience and support needs while taking responsibility for how she handled the concern.
The analyst does not need to request an acknowledgment before the supervisor examines her own decision. She can address the problem while asking how he would prefer his contribution to be recognized.

The supervisor takes responsibility for the decision and explains what will change. Checking the analyst’s preference about acknowledgment avoids making public recognition another condition he must accept. The follow-through matters more than a promise that trust is restored.
lessons.reflection: Think of a team where you felt free to disagree. What did the leader or group do that made that possible? Which of those habits do you practice yourself?
lessons.action: In your next meeting, try one practice: ask for the strongest case against a proposal, or close by saying one thing that changed because someone raised it. Notice what happens.

check.question: Which statement best describes psychological safety as Edmondson defined it?
check.correct: A shared belief among team members that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking.
wrong: A policy that guarantees no one will ever feel uncomfortable at work.
A personality trait of confident employees who speak up easily.
check.feedback: Edmondson's definition is about a team-level belief shaped by how the group behaves. It does not promise comfort, and it is not a trait of individuals. Discomfort is normal when learning. The question is whether speaking up is punished.

lessons.title: Reporting routes: route, do not investigate
objectives: Identify the internal and external routes for raising respectful workplace, harassment and discrimination concerns.
Explain supervisors' immediate reporting and referral responsibilities without substituting an independent inquiry for the authorized process.
Describe what retaliation is and why it is prohibited.
Draft a brief, factual referral that shares only what is needed.
lessons.teaching:
Support and reporting serve different needs when someone raises a workplace concern. Policy 1432 identifies supervisors, Human Resources, union representatives and the Employee Assistance Program as possible contacts for respectful workplace concerns. A conversation with a union representative or EAP may provide support, but it does not replace a report required by DHS policy. The published DHS policy expects employees to report complaints of discrimination, harassment or retaliation promptly to a supervisor or the Equal Opportunity and Access Division (EOAD). Employees may also contact the Minnesota Department of Human Rights or the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, whose filing rules and deadlines apply separately.

Supervisors have added duties when they learn of an allegation based on a protected class, such as disability. Policy 1436 requires an immediate report to HR or the agency affirmative action officer under agency procedures. DHS policy also directs supervisors to refer complaints promptly to EOAD and consult the division about a response. Listen, explain the referral and ask about immediate support needs without first interviewing witnesses or deciding whether the allegation is credible. EOAD assesses the complaint and investigates when warranted; supervisors must cooperate with that process.

An informal conversation is not a substitute for a required referral. DHS policy allows informal options, including a facilitated conversation requested through EOAD. A person need not try those options before filing a formal complaint. These choices do not authorize a supervisor to investigate independently or postpone a report while trying to settle the concern privately.

DHS policy prohibits retaliation for reporting discrimination or harassment, opposing discriminatory conduct, seeking disability or religious accommodations, or taking part in an investigation. A change in assignments or meeting access may raise a concern about retaliation, but the example by itself does not prove a violation. Describe the specific conduct and relevant context so the person or area responsible can assess what happened.

Before someone shares details, explain what your role requires you to report and the limits of confidentiality. Make factual notes, protect the information and share it only with people who need it for an authorized purpose. The public policy copy uses an earlier division name, so check current contacts and procedures on the DHS intranet. If the route is unclear, consult HR or EOAD promptly rather than delaying a required report.
lessons.keyPoint: DHS employees are expected to report complaints promptly through the designated agency channels. Supervisors must follow their additional reporting and referral duties while explaining confidentiality limits and asking about immediate support needs.
lessons.example: Practice case: A DSD unit supervisor is approached by a case management consultant, who says a colleague has made repeated comments about his disability and has joked about his accommodation in front of others. The consultant asks the supervisor to keep it between them and just talk to the colleague informally. The supervisor wants to respect the consultant's wishes and fix the problem quickly.
lessons.question: What should the supervisor do?
choices: Thank the consultant, explain the required referral to Equal Opportunity and Access, ask about immediate support needs, and make the referral promptly under DHS procedures.
Agree to keep it confidential and speak to the colleague informally to stop the jokes.
Interview the coworkers who were present to confirm the consultant's account before deciding whether to refer it.
feedback: This response follows the referral duty while keeping the consultant informed about the next step. The supervisor asks about support without promising confidentiality, a particular finding, or protection she cannot guarantee.

Promising secrecy conflicts with the supervisor's referral responsibility. The supervisor should explain confidentiality limits and refer the complaint promptly, even if the consultant prefers an informal response.

Referral should not wait for the supervisor to verify the account herself. Equal Opportunity and Access determines the appropriate response, and the supervisor must cooperate with any authorized investigation.
lessons.reflection: If someone brought you a concern tomorrow, would you know which route fits? What would you need to look up or ask so you feel prepared?
lessons.action: Find and save the current contact route for DHS EOAD, your HR business partner and the Employee Assistance Program. If you supervise, review with HR what your referral duty looks like in practice.

check.question: Why should a supervisor refer a protected-class harassment complaint promptly instead of first deciding whether it is true?
check.correct: Because referral allows the authorized process to assess the complaint without the supervisor delaying it through an independent inquiry.
wrong: Because supervisors are not allowed to listen to complaints at all.
Because referral is only needed when the supervisor believes the complaint is true.
check.feedback: The supervisor should listen, explain the referral, and ask about immediate support needs. Referral does not depend on the supervisor first deciding whether the account is true; Equal Opportunity and Access determines the appropriate response under DHS procedures.

cards.back: Unwelcome conduct based on a protected characteristic that becomes a condition of employment or is severe or pervasive enough to create a hostile work environment.
Statewide and DHS policy covering disrespectful conduct such as shouting, bullying and demeaning treatment, including conduct that is not tied to a protected class.
Distract, delegate, document, delay and direct: five bystander options taught by Right To Be. Consider safety and the targeted person’s wishes while following workplace reporting and records duties.
Edmondson's term for a shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk taking, such as asking questions, admitting mistakes or disagreeing.
Negative treatment because someone reports or opposes discrimination or harassment, takes part in an investigation, or requests a disability or religious accommodation. DHS policy prohibits it.
The DHS Equal Opportunity and Access Division receives and assesses discrimination, harassment and retaliation complaints and investigates when warranted.

aid.heading: When you witness something
items: Check safety first, for the targeted person and for you.
Pick one of the five Ds: distract, delegate, document, delay or direct.
Check in afterward and ask what the person needs.
Ask about support and documentation preferences, explain applicable reporting and records responsibilities, and share information through authorized channels.
Do not investigate. Route the concern.

aid.heading: If someone brings you a concern
items: Listen, thank them and avoid judging whether it is serious enough.
Explain honestly what you can and cannot keep confidential.
Distinguish agency reporting routes from support available through a union representative or the Employee Assistance Program. External agencies have separate processes.
Follow the reporting duties for your role. Supervisors must follow their additional immediate reporting and referral responsibilities.
Watch for and route any retaliation.

aid.heading: Team habits that build safety
items: Ask for the strongest case against your own idea before deciding.
Acknowledge useful contributions in a way the person is comfortable with.
Offer information and a chance to learn without treating lack of intent as a reason to bypass reporting duties.
When something lands badly, the person with more power leads the repair.
Say what changed because someone spoke up.

sources.title: U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission — Harassment
sources.note: Supports the federal definition of harassment, the protected characteristics, the condition-of-employment and severe-or-pervasive standards, and the note that petty slights are usually not illegal. Federal enforcement positions change, so check current EEOC guidance for any formal question.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Rights — Minnesota Human Rights Act
sources.note: Supports the list of protected classes in employment under Minnesota law, including sexual orientation and gender identity, and the reprisal protection. Formal determinations rest with MDHR and the courts.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — HR/LR Policy 1432, Respectful Workplace (revised 2023)
sources.note: Supports the statewide definition of respectful conduct, examples of disrespectful behavior, the separation from protected-class harassment, and reporting routes including supervisor, HR, union representative and EAP.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — HR/LR Policy 1436, Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited (revised 2024)
sources.note: Supports examples of protected-class harassment including deliberate misgendering and name mispronunciation, supervisor duty to report immediately, and the retaliation prohibition.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services — Discrimination, Harassment and Retaliation Policy
sources.note: Supports employee reporting expectations, supervisors' prompt referral and consultation responsibilities, and the role of Equal Opportunity and Access in assessing and investigating complaints. The public copy uses an earlier organizational name; confirm current procedures and contacts on the DHS intranet.

sources.title: Right To Be — The 5Ds of Bystander Intervention
sources.note: Supports the five bystander strategies and the guidance to ask the targeted person before using any documentation. The workplace adaptations in this course are the program's own.

sources.title: Edmondson, A. — Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams, Administrative Science Quarterly (1999)
sources.note: Supports the definition of team psychological safety and its association with learning behavior in a field study of work teams. Findings are associational. The practice list in lesson three comes from program-owned material.
